Alright sir — I’ll explain these topics the way your exam expects (logical + application- based) , not just definitions. I’ll go step by step with intuition + how questions are framed. 🔹 1. What are Design Rules (Core Idea) From your notes Pasted text Design rules = ways to make systems usable But they differ in authority vs generality : Type Meaning Use in Questions Principles General ideas “Which usability principle is violated?” Guidelines Suggestions “Suggest improvements” Standards Strict rules “Is this design compliant?” 👉 Exam trick: If strict rule → Standard If broad idea → Principle If suggestion → Guideline 🔹 2. 3 Core Usability Principles (VERY IMPORTANT) These are the backbone — almost every logical question comes from here. 🟢 (A) Learnability 👉 “Can a new user understand system easily?” Sub-parts: 1. Predictability User can guess what will happen 📌 Example: Button says “Delete” → file should delete If it opens settings → ❌ not predictable 👉 Question type: User clicks button but unexpected result happens → which principle violated? ✔ Answer: Predictability 2. Synthesizability User understands what already happened 📌 Example: After saving → “File saved successfully” No feedback → ❌ bad 👉 Logical: System must show effect of past actions 3. Familiarity Use real-world knowledge 📌 Example: Trash icon for delete Folder structure like OS 👉 If user has to “learn from scratch” → bad design 4. Generalizability Learning in one place works elsewhere 📌 Example: Ctrl+C works everywhere 5. Consistency Same action → same result 📌 Example: Save button sometimes saves, sometimes deletes → ❌ 🟡 (B) Flexibility 👉 “Different ways to interact with system” 1. Dialogue Initiative User controls system (not system controlling user) 📌 Example: Can skip steps → good Forced wizard → bad 2. Multithreading Multiple tasks at once 📌 Example: Download + browsing simultaneously 3. Task Migratability Task shifts between user & system 📌 Example: Autofill forms (system helps) 4. Substitutivity Multiple ways to do same task 📌 Example: Shortcut OR mouse click 5. Customizability User can change interface 📌 Example: Dark mode, layout change 🔴 (C) Robustness 👉 “How well system supports user during use” 1. Observability User can see system state 📌 Example: Loading bar, status indicators 2. Recoverability User can fix mistakes 📌 Example: Undo button 👉 If no undo → major violation 3. Responsiveness System reacts quickly 📌 Example: Laggy UI → bad 4. Task Conformance System supports actual user tasks 📌 Example: Calculator without divide → useless 🔥 How Questions Are Asked (IMPORTANT) Sir, your professor will NOT ask definitions. Expect: ✅ Example 1: User deletes file accidentally and cannot undo ✔ Concept → Recoverability ✅ Example 2: User presses button but no feedback appears ✔ Concept → Synthesizability / Observability ✅ Example 3: Same action behaves differently in different screens ✔ Concept → Consistency ✅ Example 4: System forces user to follow fixed steps ✔ Concept → Dialogue Initiative (low flexibility) 🔹 3. Standards vs Guidelines (Easy marks) 🟢 Standards Strict rules (ISO etc.) Example: ISO 9241 👉 Defines usability as: Effectiveness Efficiency Satisfaction 🟡 Guidelines Suggestions Used in design improvement 👉 Example: “Use simple language” “Provide feedback” 🔹 4. Golden Rules (HIGH PROBABILITY) 🟢 Ben Shneiderman – 8 Golden Rules Important ones (don’t memorize all blindly): Consistency Feedback Error prevention Undo (reversal) Reduce memory load 👉 Exam logic: If question involves: Errors → prevention/recovery Memory → reduce cognitive load Repetition → consistency 🟡 Don Norman – 7 Principles Important: Visibility Mapping Constraints Design for error 👉 Example: If user can’t understand system → visibility problem 🔹 5. Design Patterns (Conceptual but asked indirectly) 👉 Reusable solutions to common problems 📌 Example: “Go back button” “Search bar on top” 👉 Question type: Why reuse design patterns? ✔ Answer: Saves time Proven solutions Improves usability 🔥 Final Exam Strategy (Very Important) Sir, here’s how you solve ANY question: 1. Identify issue: Learning issue → Learnability Control issue → Flexibility Error/feedback issue → Robustness 2. Match sub-concept: No undo → Recoverability Confusing UI → Predictability/Familiarity No feedback → Observability/Synthesizability If you want next: 👉 I’ll give 10 exam-level logical questions (with solutions) 👉 Or we can do dangerous states topic next (your previous ask) Sources Sources

Device Independence 👉 Same code works on different hardware 📌 Example: Mouse / touch → same app works 👉 Question: Why abstraction needed? ✔ Answer: portability + hardware independence 2. Resource Sharing 👉 Multiple apps run together 📌 Example: Browser + music + IDE 👉 If system allows only one app → ❌ no resource sharing 🟡 Architectures (VERY ASKED) 1. App handles everything Hard to manage Low portability ❌ 2. OS kernel handles Tied to OS ❌ 3. Separate manager (BEST) High portability ✔ 👉 Exam question: Which architecture is best? ✔ Answer: Separate manager 🟣 Example System 👉 X Window System Client-server model Server handles display Client = application 🔥 3. Programming Models (VERY IMPORTANT) 🟢 (A) Event Loop Model while(true){ read event process event } 👉 System continuously checks events 📌 Example: Game loop Low-level UI 🟡 (B) Notification (Callback) Model button.onClick = saveFunction 👉 Event triggers function 📌 Example: Java Swing, Android ⚔️ Comparison (Exam gold) Case Better Model Modal dialog Event loop Case Better Model Non-modal UI Notification 👉 Logical question: Why event loop bad for complex UI? ✔ Hard to manage many states 🔹 4. Toolkits (Easy but important) 👉 Provide ready UI components 📌 Example: Buttons, menus, sliders 🟢 Key Idea 👉 “Don’t code UI from scratch” 🟡 Advantages Consistency ✔ Faster development ✔ Reusable ✔ 🟣 Example: 👉 Java AWT 👉 Java Swing 🔥 5. UIMS (VERY IMPORTANT CONCEPT) 👉 Full form: User Interface Management System 🟢 Core Idea 👉 Separate: UI (Presentation) ≠ Logic (Application) 🟡 Why? Benefit Meaning Portability run anywhere Reusability reuse UI Customization change UI easily 🔥 Exam Question Why separation important? ✔ Because UI changes frequently, logic doesn’t 🔹 6. Seeheim Model (HIGH PROBABILITY) 🟢 Structure Presentation → Dialogue → Application 🧠 Meaning Layer Role Presentation UI Dialogue Control interaction logic Layer Role Application core logic 📌 Example Click “Save”: Presentation → button click Dialogue → decide action Application → save file 🔥 Question Type If UI change but logic same? ✔ Only Presentation layer affected 🔹 7. MVC Model (VERY IMPORTANT) 🟢 Structure Model → Data View → UI Controller → Input handling 📌 Example Calculator: Model → numbers View → display Controller → button click 🔥 Problem (Important) 👉 Input depends on UI 📌 Example: Mouse click → need to know where user clicked 👉 So: Controller must interact with View 🔹 8. PAC Model (Conceptual but asked) 🟢 Structure Presentation Control Abstraction 🟡 Key Idea 👉 Control manages everything 👉 Better separation than MVC ⚠️ Reality MVC used more PAC cleaner but complex 🔹 9. Feedback Types (VERY IMPORTANT) 🟢 Types Type Example Lexical cursor moves Syntactic menu highlight Type Example Semantic result changes 🔥 Exam Trick 👉 Semantic feedback is slow 👉 Use fast feedback (lexical/syntactic) 📌 Example Dragging file: Highlight folder → syntactic ✔ File actually moves → semantic ✔ 🔹 10. Dialogue Control Techniques 🟢 Methods State diagrams Event handling Constraints 🔥 Important Concept 👉 Constraints = define “what should be true” 📌 Example: Password length ≥ 8 🔥 FINAL EXAM STRATEGY Sir, solve questions like this: Step 1: Identify layer UI issue → Presentation Logic issue → Application Interaction flow → Dialogue Step 2: Identify concept Problem Concept Multiple apps Windowing UI components Toolkit Separation UIMS Click handling Controller Feedback missing Observability Step 3: Match model UI + logic separation → Seeheim / MVC Event handling → Notification / Event loop 🔥 If you want next I strongly suggest: 👉 I give 10 tricky exam-level MCQs + case-based questions OR 👉 Continue with dangerous states + STN (very important for your paper) Sources Sources

BNF (Backus-Naur Form) 👉 Describes interaction as grammar 📌 Example: select → move mouse + click ⚠️ Problem: Only syntax (no meaning) Cannot detect inconsistency 2. TAG (Task Action Grammar) 👉 Improved BNF ✔ Adds meaning + consistency 📌 Example: Ensures command format same across system 🟤 (E) Physical Models (KLM – VERY IMPORTANT) 👉 Predicts time taken by user Operators: Symbol Meaning K keystroke P pointing H hand movement Symbol Meaning M thinking R system response Formula: T = TK + TP + TH + TM + TR 📌 Insight: Shortcuts faster than menus Used to compare designs ⚫ (F) Architectural Models 👉 Based on human brain structure Memory (short-term / long-term) Processing 👉 Rarely asked directly 🔥 2. Properties of Dialogue (VERY IMPORTANT) 🟢 Action Properties Property Meaning Completeness all actions defined Determinism one action → one result Consistency same action → same result 🔴 State Properties 1. Reachability 👉 Can user reach all states? 2. Reversibility 👉 Can user go back? 3. Dangerous States (VERY IMPORTANT) 👉 States user should NOT reach 📌 Example: Exit without saving → dangerous 🔥 6.
